transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Nina Ortiz (Redwood SE), Alice Chen (Acme CTO), Ravi Kumar (Lead ML Eng), Maria Gomez (Security), Ben Torres (Infra)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive focused on long-context (128k+ tokens) runtime performance, chunking strategies, KV cache behavior, batching/throughput tradeoffs, quantization impacts, and deployment options (VPC/on-prem vs hosted/dedicated). Customer shared their primary workload (medical record summarization + multi-doc retrieval chains) and performance targets (p95 latency < 8s for 2k chunk responses, sustained throughput 6-8 qps for batch inference), and expressed security/regulatory constraints to keep PHI in a VPC/on-prem lane.

Topics Covered:
- 128k context handling strategies (sparse attention, chunking, sliding window, memory indices)
- KV cache and prefix caching for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) at scale
- Batching policies: continuous batching vs fixed-time window, tail-latency mitigation
- Quantization: 8-bit/4-bit impacts on latency and QA (and recommended calibration tests)
- Dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs for throughput/cost and fallback policies
- VPC/on-prem considerations: KMS integration, audit logs, network egress/throughput

Transcript Body:
00:00 Jordan: all right everyone thanks for hopping on we wanted to run through the long context stuff, the 128k plus use case you mentioned in your brief, Alice, and make sure we cover the runtime knobs and the on prem constraints
00:12 Alice: yeah thanks, Jordan, big thing for us is the medical records pipeline, we may need the model to see like full patient histories across multiple documents, so the 128k experiments are important. latency is a concern obviously, we have some internal SLOs around p95 response times for interactive workflows
00:25 Samir: cool, quick question on the workload, is the 128k request typically a single monolithic prompt or is it the result of concatenating many smaller docs during retrieval?
00:33 Ravi: mostly retrieval concat — we do dense retrieval, then append top-N docs, but we also keep an in-memory index with recency so sometimes a single query pulls in a few hundred kilobytes of context, so effectively 100k+ tokens in many flows
00:48 Samir: okay, that matches what we've seen. For that pattern we usually recommend a hybrid approach: chunking into overlapping windows with a memory index + KV cache to avoid re-computing prefix activations. The KV cache helps a lot for repeat prefixes in multi-step RAG.
01:05 Ben: can you say more about the KV cache eviction policy? in our infra we want to bound GPU memory footprint so we need predictable worst-case usage
01:13 Nina: good point — our runtime lets you set a soft cap on KV entries per model variant and falls back to recompute when the cap is hit; you can also pin warm prefixes for hot users. Eviction is LRU by default but you can plug in a TTL or size-based policy. In practice for 128k contexts we recommend aggressively chunking larger docs and caching only the chunk boundaries and the most recent n prefixes.
01:37 Maria: on the security side, how are KV cache contents protected? if we're on dedicated or private deployment we still need to ensure PHI isn't leaked 
01:44 Samir: KV cache is in-process GPU memory on Redwood Dedicated and in the customer's VPC/on-prem deployment the cache never leaves the customer's network. We integrate with KMS for encrypting persisted checkpoints and audit log entries. For hosted pools we also isolate per-tenant and do encryption at rest. That said, we recommend configuring strict retention and TTLs for sensitive workloads.
02:05 Alice: what about quantization — we need to know accuracy tradeoffs for 4-bit vs 8-bit on summarization tasks
02:12 Samir: yes, 8-bit symmetric quant tends to give negligible quality loss for many LLMs; 4-bit (especially newer GPT-style models) can be OK but requires a calibration pass. For 128k context behavior quant impacts kernel selection — on A100/RTX-class GPUs 8-bit kernels are well optimized so latency improves but KV cache footprint changes slightly because of packed representations. We usually recommend starting with 8-bit and running a small eval set of your summarization prompts to measure ROUGE/F1 drop — we can provide a calibration harness.
02:43 Ravi: can you share numbers? like for a 128k retrieval plus generation where average output is 300 tokens, what's p95 latency and throughput on a single dedicated pod vs hosted?
02:53 Samir: rough ordering: with streaming disabled and a single dedicated 8xA100-style pod optimized for long context, you might see p95 in the 4–10s range for that pattern with good chunking & prefix caching; throughput depends on batching — sustained qps of ~6–10 when you use continuous batching and batching window tuned to 20–50ms. Hosted multi-tenant pools will have more variance; dedicated gives you predictable tail latency and the ability to pin quant/kernel configs.
03:21 Jordan: one nuance is tail-latency mitigation — we support hedging and speculative execution where small prefix results are returned while the rest of the context is still being processed; this reduces perceived latency for interactive UIs.
03:36 Ben: what's the network egress load if we do VPC/on-prem with a separate control plane? how much chatter between the control plane and nodes during inference?
03:44 Nina: for private deployments the control plane handles scheduling and metrics; actual token-level data stays on customer nodes. Network traffic is minimal during steady-state inference aside from heartbeat and metrics; if you opt-in for streaming through our control plane there is more egress but we recommend direct egress for sensitive PHI workloads.
04:02 Maria: audit logs, retention, and SSO — we'll need SOC2 artifacts and to know how audit logs look, whether they include token-level traces (we prefer not)
04:12 Samir: audit logs capture request metadata, model version, route, latencies, but not raw tokens by default; token-level traces are opt-in for debugging and stored encrypted with KMS and separate retention policy. We'll share the SOC2 package and an example log schema.
04:29 Alice: how do you deal with attention optimizations? for 128k we can't do dense attention across everything, do you support sparse attention or flash attention variants?
04:37 Samir: runtime supports a few strategies. We have distributed KV with chunked attention where attention is dense within a sliding window and sparse cross-window attention through compressed summaries. We also leverage FlashAttention kernels where beneficial; the runtime picks kernels based on sequence length distribution at request time. For extremely long docs we recommend hierarchical encoding — produce chunk embeddings, run a memory index, and only pass top candidates into the full attention layers.
05:06 Ravi: what about chunking strategies for RAG? overlapping windows vs disjoint with rerank?
05:13 Nina: both have tradeoffs. Overlapping windows produce better context continuity but increase compute; disjoint windows plus reranking is cheaper but you need a good reranker to avoid losing context. We often combine: disjoint chunking for initial retrieval, then overlap around top-k chunks and use KV cache to avoid recompute across rounds.
05:35 Jordan: we put a link in the chat to our benchmark sheet and a short note on recommended chunk sizes per model family — that'll help you tune.
05:43 Samir: another tip: for shallow generation (short outputs) bundling multiple requests in a micro-batch drastically improves throughput without much latency penalty. For deep generations (long outputs) batching is less effective because decoding becomes the bottleneck.
06:05 Ben: curious about fallback policies — if dedicated capacity is saturated can traffic be spilled to hosted variants? what's the privacy implication?
06:14 Jordan: yes, we support configurable fallbacks where you can specify acceptable fallback model families and whether to allow fallback to hosted pools. For PHI-heavy workloads we recommend no-host fallback and instead a burst-on-prem option or pre-provisioned spare nodes. Fallback is controlled by route policy and can be audited.
06:33 Maria: on KMS — can you support our on-prem HSM?
06:37 Samir: yes, we integrate with external KMS/HSM via standard interfaces; for Private deployments the keys never leave your HSM. We'll need to validate network connectivity and an access pattern but it's supported.
06:49 Alice: what's the recommended test plan to validate quality + perf for our 128k pipeline?
06:54 Samir: two-phase: run functional evals with representative prompts to measure quality delta across quant configs (8-bit/4-bit) and model variants, then run load tests with a subset of real retrieval traces to measure p50/p95/p99 and GPU memory pressure. We can run an initial benchmark on Redwood Dedicated staging and share raw logs so you can review.
07:20 Ravi: can you include the exact kernel & runtime flags you used in the benchmarks? we want reproducibility
07:25 Samir: yes we'll include kernel versions, quant flags, batch window sizes, and the exact chunking script. We'll attach the harness to the benchmark sheet.
07:33 Jordan: recap of next steps — Samir will run end-to-end benchmark with Acme's sample dataset; Jordan will send pricing + pilot plan; Nina will share private deployment checklist and network diagram; Maria will get SOC2 and KMS integration docs.
07:50 Alice: great thank you, this was helpful. one last thing — can we get a short write-up about latency-vs-cost tradeoffs for 128k so our execs can decide dedicated vs on prem?
07:58 Jordan: yes we'll put together a 1-pager with cost estimates and expected tail-latency buckets per deployment mode.
